links.mech: Restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, shut-in production among Gulf oil producers, and attacks on bypass pipelines cut crude supply and push Brent prices up.
If Gulf oil exports, excluding Iran's, fall below half their normal level, global supply shrinks sharply and oil prices spike again.
An end to the war and a full reopening would bring Gulf production and exports back, pulling oil prices down.
With the Strait of Hormuz, which used to carry about a fifth of the world's LNG, shut and Qatar's production facilities under attack, Asian spot LNG prices rise.
Continued attacks on and seizures of merchant ships in the strait and Gulf waters drive up war-risk insurance premiums and tanker rates.

When the Houthis threaten Saudi ports and Red Sea shipping, more vessels avoid the Suez route, pushing up freight rates and insurance premiums, and exports from Yanbu, the route around Hormuz, also come under threat.
South Korea imports most of its crude, so higher oil prices raise its import bill and strain its current account, pushing the won-dollar exchange rate up (a weaker won).
Higher oil prices lift the prices of gasoline, diesel, and other petroleum products first, then spread to other goods through transport and production costs.
links.num: Dubai crude +10% → consumer price inflation +0.20 pp (KDI)

links.mech: Rising consumer prices erode South Korean households' real purchasing power and weigh most on households that spend a large share of their budgets on fuel and transportation.

When the loss of Gulf LNG drives up Asian LNG prices, European gas prices (TTF) rise with them, since Europe competes for the same cargoes (the two prices have a correlation coefficient of 0.8, according to the IEA), raising heating and electricity bills and consumer prices in Germany, Poland, and elsewhere.
Higher European gas and energy prices raise electricity and fuel bills and consumer prices in Italy, Spain, Greece, and other countries.

When the loss of Gulf LNG lifts gas prices in Europe and Asia, Russia's Yamal LNG, sold under price-linked contracts, earns more, increasing Russia's gas export revenue. Higher volumes contribute little, and the link weakens sharply once the EU ban on imports under long-term contracts takes effect in January 2027.

Higher Brent prices raise the price of Russia's Urals crude and the mineral extraction tax revenue tied to it, increasing Russia's earnings from exports of crude and petroleum products. A stronger ruble and compensation payments to domestic refiners, however, may keep ruble-denominated budget revenue from rising as much (oil and gas budget revenue fell 17.2 percent year on year from January through September 2026).

If oil and gas revenue holds up, Russia faces less fiscal pressure to make concessions at the negotiating table, which could prolong the war of attrition. Confidence is low, however: Russia's revenue from sources other than oil and gas is far larger, and extra revenue could fund a more aggressive course rather than simply sustain attrition.
If the Iran war keeps oil prices high, a year in which Brent averages below $60 a barrel becomes less likely.
When oil prices spike, Washington puts securing supply ahead of pressuring buyers of Russian oil, making it less likely to enforce tariffs on those buyers.
If diesel prices stay high, the U.S. Treasury has more reason to extend or broaden General License 135, which covers Russian diesel.
Sustained high oil prices increase U.S. shale producers' revenue and their incentive to drill, raising output.

Higher LNG prices in Asia and Europe lift the selling price and margins of U.S. LNG, increasing U.S. LNG companies' profits. Export volumes depend more on when new facilities come online than on prices.

To fend off Iranian missile and drone attacks, the United States is firing Patriot and THAAD interceptors faster than it can produce them and shifting air-defense forces and munitions from the Indo-Pacific to the Middle East, leaving fewer stocks and deployed forces for other theaters. Estimates of the drawdown vary (CSIS put Patriot use at 759 to 827 missiles as of late July; CNN reported that about 50 percent of Patriot and about 80 percent of THAAD stocks had been used, which the defense secretary denied), and stocks are estimated to recover around 2029.
The cutoff of Gulf urea fertilizer that used to pass through the Strait of Hormuz drives up fertilizer prices and raises production costs for U.S. corn farmers.

When risks in Middle Eastern waters force ships to reroute and freight rates rise, South Korean shipping companies that operate tankers and container ships earn more. If Gulf ports close and cargo volumes themselves fall, carriers on those routes may take losses.

As Ukraine keeps using up U.S.-made Patriot interceptors and precision munitions in its war with Russia, U.S. stocks shrink, and Washington slows transfers to protect supplies needed for other theaters.
As U.S. interceptor stocks shrink, fewer Patriots reach Ukraine, so Russian ballistic missiles hit more Ukrainian cities and power and heating facilities, causing greater harm to Ukrainians.

The smaller U.S. interceptor stocks become, the stronger Washington's incentive to put its own needs first and delay or halt deliveries of Patriots and other weapons to Ukraine. Transfers continued in 2026 at an average of 12 missiles a month, however, so it is uncertain whether this would lead to a halt of more than 30 days.

If U.S. air-defense stocks run short, interceptors and air-defense munitions held by U.S. Forces Korea are moved to the Middle East and elsewhere, and with stocks not recovering until around 2029, the situation edges toward a substantive U.S. retreat unless something fills the gap. Confidence is low: the THAAD system has stayed in South Korea, the munitions moves may be temporary, and a substantive U.S. retreat requires troop cuts or weaker commitments to be made official.

If interceptor shortages become a pretext for delaying arms deliveries to Taiwan, and the delayed sales are then used as a bargaining chip with China, the situation moves closer to the Taiwan issue's external variable of the United States postponing arms sales to Taiwan for the sake of negotiations with China.

As U.S. stocks flow to the Middle East, deliveries of U.S. munitions that Baltic and Scandinavian countries bought through Foreign Military Sales slip, and some Patriots in Europe are pulled out, widening defense gaps in countries that border Russia. For these gaps to become a military threat their people actually face, Russia would need both the intent and the capacity to exploit them.

When U.S. air-defense stocks and production fall short, countries that urgently need interceptors turn to South Korean air-defense systems with faster delivery, such as the Cheongung-II surface-to-air missile, and South Korean defense firms receive more requests for orders. South Korea's production capacity is also tied up by existing contracts, however (the government has told the UAE it would be difficult to meet its request for early supply), so how much orders actually grow depends on how fast production expands.

With interceptors scarce, the United States has less capacity to stop Iranian retaliatory missiles, which tilts it toward putting off a resumption of large-scale strikes on mainland Iran. Here shortages restrain escalation, contrary to the conventional view that heavier attrition pushes a country to seek a quick, decisive battle.

If Russian or Belarusian actions kill people on NATO territory or a Russian manned aircraft is shot down, eastern member states raise their air-defense and border-defense budgets further and call for joint EU funding.
As long as Russia's war continues, European countries treat Russia as a long-term threat and raise defense spending over several years.

Rising European defense spending lifts demand for South Korean land weapons, which compete on fast delivery. Procurement funded by the EU caps the share of components from outside the bloc, however, so contracts come with conditions for local production and technology transfer.

European naval buildups have raised hopes of more submarine and warship exports for South Korean shipbuilders, but European countries favor cooperation within Europe and the participation of their own industries, so little of this turns into actual orders.
When European allies use larger defense budgets to buy U.S. weapons for Ukraine, U.S. defense companies sell more.
Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil export terminals and pipelines cut Russia's crude export volumes, eroding part of its windfall from high oil prices.
If Washington widens or extends exemptions from its sanctions on Russian oil, Russian oil sells in more markets at higher prices, increasing Russia's export revenue.

Higher oil and gas revenue lets the Russian government draw less on its sovereign wealth fund, delaying the point at which it reaches the limits of its war finances (the fund's liquid assets falling below 1 trillion rubles, or new emergency measures such as limits on bank withdrawals). In 2026, though, the projected budget deficit widened to 3.2 percent of GDP despite higher oil prices, so this link has limited force.
When Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries cut Russia's diesel exports, global diesel margins rise, lifting profits for South Korean refiners, which export a large share of their diesel.

When Russia brings in artillery shells, missiles, and troops from North Korea for its war, North Korea gains hard currency, energy, and military technology along with combat experience, and military cooperation between the two deepens.

If a full Russia-Ukraine ceasefire holds, Russia needs fewer shells and troops, and North Korea earns less from arms exports and troop deployments. The 2024 North Korea-Russia mutual defense treaty and their technology cooperation would remain, however.

As North Korea tests its missiles in combat on Russian battlefields, improving their accuracy and gaining experience operating drones, the military threat to South Koreans grows, since the same weapons can be aimed at South Korea's command facilities, airfields, and ports.

While it gets money and technology from Russia, North Korea has little incentive to deal with Washington for sanctions relief; if Russian demand falls, it may seek a deal with the United States again. Because North Korea excludes South Korea as a negotiating partner, talks opened this way would look like a deal without South Korea.
As Russian airstrikes target Ukrainian cities and energy facilities and the burden of conscription grows, Ukrainians keep migrating to Europe.

A continued influx of refugees increases demand for housing, welfare, and education in the western, central, and eastern European countries that take in the most, and fuels political backlash over the burden of hosting them.

If the EU cuts off Russian LNG imports because of the war in Ukraine, Europe has to buy replacement cargoes on the global spot market, competing with Asia for the same shipments, which tends to push up Asian LNG prices (JKM).

When Asian LNG prices (JKM) rise, South Korea, which imports nearly all of its LNG, sees Korea Gas Corporation's import costs climb along with the wholesale power price (the system marginal price), which is tied to the cost of LNG-fired generation. That increases pressure to raise gas and electricity rates and widens state utilities' losses and unrecovered costs. Because much of the LNG is bought under oil-linked long-term contracts, the direct effect of JKM is limited to the spot share, and the government offsets part of it by easing limits on coal-fired generation and restarting nuclear reactors to cut gas use.

If access to Taiwan's major ports is blocked for seven days or more, shipments of LNG for power generation and of process materials stop, and utilization falls at TSMC, which keeps most of its advanced production in Taiwan.

If fighting breaks out between Chinese forces and Taiwanese or U.S. forces, the risk grows that fabs in western Taiwan and sea and air logistics halt together, and the supply of advanced chips plunges.
When Taiwanese foundry output falls, shipments from U.S. fabless companies, such as Nvidia, that rely on TSMC for wafer production and CoWoS packaging fall accordingly.

When the supply of advanced chips shrinks, U.S. electronics and hardware companies that rely on Taiwanese partners for components and assembly produce less, and finding alternative suppliers takes months or longer.
If Taiwan's foundries stop, production of AI accelerators, the biggest market for South Korean memory chips, stops too, cutting demand for South Korean memory, including HBM.
When Taiwanese foundry output falls, supplies of automotive chips dry up, and South Korean automakers halt or cut production at their plants.

If sudden upheaval takes the form of an armed clash on the Korean Peninsula that kills 100 or more people, concerns grow over supply from Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, which together account for nearly two-thirds of global DRAM revenue, raising procurement costs and the risk of production disruptions for U.S. chip companies that use South Korean memory. A change of supreme leader alone does not open this link.
If an escalated war with Iran drags on, the United States uses up Patriot and THAAD interceptors faster than it can produce them, and its air-defense forces stay deployed in the Middle East.
If U.S. forces enter combat in the Taiwan Strait, interceptors, carriers, and air-defense forces concentrate in the western Pacific, leaving fewer stocks for other theaters.

As interceptor stocks shrink, U.S. government replenishment orders turn into multiyear production contracts, increasing orders and capital investment at U.S. defense and aerospace companies (PAC-3 MSE output from 600 to 2,000 a year, THAAD from 96 to 400 a year). Orders rise within months, but reaching production targets takes years, and the January 2026 agreement to expand production stemmed from consumption before the Iran war.

When U.S. munitions and air-defense stocks shrink and U.S. forces stay in the Middle East, China may judge the cost of gray-zone pressure, such as inspecting Taiwanese ships, to be lower, raising the probability of gray-zone escalation somewhat.

As the Russia-Ukraine war of attrition continues, Russia's demand for shells, missiles, and troops persists, expanding North Korea's arms exports and troop deployments to Russia, along with the Russian technology and fuel it receives in return.

If an unguaranteed ceasefire holds for a year or more, demand for shells and missiles falls, but North Korea's cooperation may continue in other forms, such as sending construction workers and trading technology, so the decline is modest.

The more technology, fuel, and hard currency North Korea gets from Russia, the less it stands to gain from inter-Korean steps such as restoring military communication lines or holding family reunions, lowering the probability of managed coexistence.

When Russia, a permanent member of the UN Security Council, trades arms with North Korea, it blocks monitoring of sanctions on Pyongyang (it vetoed the renewal of the panel of experts in March 2024) and treats North Korean denuclearization as a closed issue, weakening the enforcement power of the nuclear nonproliferation regime. But China and Russia were already casting vetoes in May 2022, before the arms trade began, so much of the weakening stems from a common cause: the confrontation between the United States and Russia.

If Iran declares its withdrawal from the NPT or begins enriching uranium to 90 percent, the nonproliferation regime's normative force weakens; a withdrawal would make Iran the second country to leave the treaty, after North Korea in 2003.

Iran is a member of the NPT, so an Iranian nuclear test or a formal declaration that it has nuclear weapons would itself breach its NPT obligations and immediately weaken the treaty's binding force. It would also strengthen the motives of Saudi Arabia and other Middle Eastern states to acquire nuclear weapons, weakening that force further.

If the UN Security Council fails to impose new sanctions after a seventh North Korean nuclear test, it signals that nuclear tests cost little, eroding the deterrent force of the nonproliferation regime.

The weaker confidence in U.S. extended deterrence becomes, the greater the pressure on South Korea or Japan to formalize a decision to develop nuclear weapons, withdraw from the NPT, or abandon its non-nuclear principles.

If the United States formally announces cuts of 10 percent or more to its authorized troop levels in South Korea and Japan, or withdraws its policy of providing defensive weapons to Taiwan, South Korea and Japan will rate the credibility of U.S. extended deterrence lower.

If South Korea formalizes a decision to develop nuclear weapons or withdraw from the NPT, the possibility of financial sanctions under U.S. law is priced in as a risk to won assets, pushing the won-dollar exchange rate up.
If going nuclear formally leads to U.S. sanctions, export licenses for U.S. engines and components are cut off, halting the production and export of South Korean weapons that use U.S. parts.

As confidence in U.S. extended deterrence weakens, European countries raise defense spending to deepen ties with France's nuclear deterrent and to expand conventional capabilities such as early warning, air defense, and long-range strike. The effect of a U.S. retreat from Asia on European allies' confidence is indirect, however.
An armed clash on the Korean Peninsula that kills 100 or more people would drive foreign money out, sending the won plunging and the won-dollar exchange rate up.

When the won-dollar exchange rate rises, the won price of imported raw materials, petroleum products, and food goes up, lifting South Korean consumer prices with a lag. The Bank of Korea estimates that a 10 percent rise in the annual average exchange rate adds 0.35 percentage point to annual consumer price inflation, with the pass-through peaking after nine months (the Hyundai Research Institute puts it at 0.3 to 0.5 percentage point). When oil prices and the exchange rate rise together, the upward pressure is greater.
links.num: Won-dollar rate +10% → consumer price inflation +0.35 pp, peaking after 9 months (Bank of Korea)

links.mech: A higher won-dollar exchange rate raises the won cost of fuel and aircraft leases paid in dollars and of foreign-currency debt, cutting South Korean airlines' earnings.

If the United States and China fight in the Taiwan Strait, U.S. bases in South Korea could become Chinese targets if they are used for Taiwan operations, and North Korea could treat the movement of U.S. forces off the peninsula as an opening for provocation, raising the probability of sudden upheaval on the Korean Peninsula.

As the NPT regime's binding force weakens, that is, as NPT withdrawals or nuclear tests go by without new Security Council sanctions and as other members such as Iran move toward withdrawal or nuclear weapons, calls in South Korea or Japan to formally withdraw from the NPT or develop nuclear weapons gain legitimacy, adding to the pressure toward nuclear dominoes. But the costs South Korea would bear come mainly from U.S. law and the alliance, and the gap at the Security Council created by China and Russia shielding North Korea does not lower those costs. South Korea's nuclear debate therefore hinges mainly on the credibility of U.S. extended deterrence, and this link carries little weight.

If an unguaranteed ceasefire stops the fighting on the Ukrainian front, Russia gains room to rebuild its troops and equipment and turn them toward NATO's eastern members, raising the chance that it tests the alliance by seizing part of their territory or launching limited strikes. That room is greater under a ceasefire with only monitors than under one with Western troops deployed.

The lower-tensions scenario for Russia and NATO requires a ceasefire in Ukraine, so an unguaranteed ceasefire, if reached, meets its first condition. It is one of several ways to meet it (a guaranteed ceasefire or a favorable end to the war would also do so). Lower tensions also require new risk-reduction mechanisms and fewer incidents on the eastern flank, sustained together for a year or more, and if any event amounting to a deadly incident, a Kaliningrad blockade crisis, limited use of force, or full-scale war occurs even once through 2030, the classification rules out lower tensions. The same ceasefire raises both the risk of limited use of force and the chance of lower tensions, but the two scenarios are mutually exclusive.

More North Korean shells, missiles, and troops let Russia sustain the intensity of its shelling and replace its losses, prolonging the war of attrition. A large increase in supply, however, could tip the war not toward continued attrition but toward a Russian breakthrough that collapses the front or peace on Russia's terms, and if North Korea's stockpiles run down and supply falls, the effect weakens. Together with the link through which attrition boosts North Korean supply, this forms a feedback loop.

If Taiwan's major ports are blocked for seven days or more, container ships and other large vessels using the Taiwan Strait and nearby routes reroute or wait, raising freight rates and war-risk insurance premiums on East Asian routes.

If the Iran war drags on in escalated form, U.S. forces are likely to keep fighting in the Middle East beyond the end of 2027, and pressure to move more Indo-Pacific forces there grows, making the Taiwan issue's external variable of a prolonged Middle East war draining U.S. forces more likely. The two definitions do not describe the same event, however: the prolonged, escalated war scenario classifies the state of affairs at the end of 2030 and includes a standoff in which shipping continues only under U.S. escort, while the external variable requires both combat past the end of 2027 and further moves of Indo-Pacific forces. The external variable can also hold if fighting lasts into 2028 and a deal before 2030 produces an end of the war and full reopening or an incomplete reopening, or if the outcome is classified as regime collapse or civil war in Iran or the collapse of Gulf exports.

One branch of the Taiwan issue's external variable of U.S. retrenchment in the region, a formal announcement of cuts of 10 percent or more to authorized troop levels in South Korea, would satisfy the Korean Peninsula issue's external variable of a substantive U.S. retreat if the cuts are actually carried out and nothing makes up for them. Retrenchment is met by the announcement alone, while a substantive retreat requires implementation, so there is a lag between them, and if compensating measures follow, a substantive retreat is not met. Conversely, a substantive retreat has no 10 percent threshold and can also be met by a formal weakening of extended deterrence, so it can occur without retrenchment. The other branches of retrenchment (cuts to U.S. forces in Japan, or withdrawing the policy on arms for Taiwan) do not overlap with a substantive retreat.
If Taiwan's major ports are blocked for seven days or more, the Korean Peninsula issue's external variable of a cross-strait crisis (a blockade or quarantine of Taiwan, or armed conflict) is met.
Deadly fighting between Chinese forces and Taiwanese or U.S. forces meets the Korean Peninsula issue's external variable of a cross-strait crisis.

If North Korea's exports of troops and shells stop after the Russia-Ukraine war ends or a long-term truce takes hold, North Korea's foreign military cooperation shrinks accordingly. Other strands of its arms and technology trade, such as deals with Iran and Russian technology transfers, may continue.

If 10,000 or more regular North Korean troops are newly deployed to Russia or occupied territory (the North Korean branch of the external variable of North Korea and China expanding support for Russia), North Korea's foreign military cooperation grows. The Chinese branch (transfers of finished weapons) has no bearing on it.

A prolonged halt to shipping at the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb flashpoint meets one branch of the Iran issue's external variable of Hormuz bypass routes being cut off. Yanbu, the outlet of Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline, lies on the Red Sea coast north of Bab el-Mandeb, so if the strait is closed, crude from Yanbu bound for Asia loses its outlet, and only volumes heading to Europe through the Suez Canal remain.

The first branch of the Korean Peninsula issue's external variable of a substantive U.S. retreat, a formal weakening of the extended deterrence commitment, is itself an erosion of the credibility of U.S. extended deterrence. The second branch, cuts to U.S. Forces Korea without compensating measures, works in the same direction.

If at least two of three steps happen (restoring military communication lines, resuming family reunions or checks on whether relatives are alive, and a nuclear and missile freeze), the two Koreas' militaries regain a channel to head off accidental clashes, and elderly members of separated families gain a chance, in their lifetimes, to meet relatives or learn whether they are alive, easing both the military threat South Koreans face and the pain of separation. Managed coexistence requires only two of the three conditions, however, so it can also be reached without the family condition.

If Washington and Pyongyang agree on a nuclear and missile freeze or sanctions relief without South Korea, intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) that can reach the U.S. mainland may be limited while short-range missiles and tactical nuclear weapons aimed at South Korea remain. That would spread the perception that U.S. security and South Korean security move separately, eroding the credibility of U.S. extended deterrence as seen from Seoul.

If the United States agrees with North Korea, which withdrew from the NPT and has tested nuclear weapons, on a freeze or sanctions relief without denuclearization, it sets a precedent that withdrawal and testing end up costing little, and enforcement of UN sanctions on North Korea loosens, weakening the NPT regime's binding force.

If human approval steps between AI target identification and strike authorization are cut back, or strike authority is delegated in advance, the risk grows that on the Korean Peninsula, where decision times are short, a misidentification leads to a strike without human confirmation. The same risk arises if North Korea automates its nuclear counterstrike command system, raising the military threat South Koreans face from accidental clashes and escalation.

If Chinese authorities inspect or detain Taiwan-bound ships or require permits for passage, shipping lines and insurers treat the waters around Taiwan as high-risk and reroute or add premiums, raising freight rates and war-risk insurance premiums on East Asian routes.

If Chinese inspections or mandatory transit permits extend to LNG carriers bound for Taiwan, delays and some shipowners' reluctance to sail there would tighten power supply in Taiwan, which keeps only small gas reserves, threatening operations at power-hungry chip plants. Gray-zone escalation counts as having occurred with a single inspection or detention, so if inspections stop at fishing boats or individual cargo ships, this path does not open. Unlike a blockade, inspections do not stop passage itself, so the drop in supply is far smaller than under a blockade.

If the U.S.-China trade truce collapses, China could reimpose the export controls it announced on October 9, 2025, and later suspended. The external variable's definition names rare-earth controls, but controls on lithium batteries and graphite anode materials were suspended under the same announcement (No. 70), so they are likely to return as well. South Korean battery makers, which import nearly all of their anode raw materials from China, would then face licensing hurdles in sourcing materials, raising production costs and delivery risks.

If the tariff truce collapses, China could retaliate by halting or cutting purchases of U.S. soybeans, hurting sales for U.S. farmers, who have relied on China for about half of their soybean exports.
If the U.S.-China tariff war flares up again, a weaker yuan and risk aversion drive foreign money out of South Korean assets, pushing the won-dollar exchange rate up (a weaker won).

If the United States resumes large-scale strikes on mainland Iran, the risk of Iranian retaliation and threats to shipping in the strait rises, pushing Brent prices up. Announcements that strikes would stop have, conversely, pushed oil prices down.

If large-scale strikes resume, Iran retaliates with missiles and drones against U.S. bases and infrastructure in Gulf states, and fending them off drains U.S. Patriot and THAAD interceptors faster than they can be produced. How much retaliatory capability Iran retains after more than eight months of war has not been confirmed, so the scale of the drawdown is uncertain.

If the United States resumes strikes on mainland Iran, Iran keeps refusing IAEA inspections of its bombed nuclear sites, and a parliamentary bill to withdraw from the NPT gains momentum. Russian and Chinese opposition makes it hard for a referral to the UN Security Council to lead to sanctions, so refusals of inspection pile up without sanctions, weakening the NPT regime's binding force.

If Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline and loadings at Yanbu are cut off, the Saudi crude that had bypassed the Strait of Hormuz through the Red Sea drops out of the market, sending Brent prices soaring.

Attacks on Yanbu and the area around Bab el-Mandeb raise war-risk premiums for Saudi-linked tankers in the Red Sea and for ships calling at ports to the south, and more ships sail around the Cape of Good Hope instead of through Suez, pushing up freight rates as well.

If the Red Sea bypass route for Saudi crude, on which South Korean refiners have relied since Hormuz was blocked, is cut off, they must bring in substitute crude at higher freight and insurance costs, and with two to three months between contract and delivery, the risk grows that deliveries will fall a few months later, raising refiners' feedstock costs and the strain on their operations. If global refining margins rise at the same time, the hit to earnings is smaller.

If Congress restricts military action against Iran through legislation or appropriations, strikes on Iran and the interceptors spent on Iranian retaliation decline, and carriers and air-defense forces held in the Middle East may return to their original theaters, giving U.S. munitions and air-defense stocks and overseas deployments more slack. Rebuilding stocks already spent depends on production rates, so the effect plays out over several years.

If Congress restricts military action against Iran through legislation or appropriations, it becomes harder for U.S. forces to keep fighting in the Middle East beyond the end of 2027 or to move more Indo-Pacific forces there, making the Taiwan issue's external variable of a prolonged Middle East war draining U.S. forces less likely. But congressional restraint covers restrictions through the end of 2028, while that external variable requires combat past the end of 2027, so this link works only if the restrictions take hold by around 2027. If the restrictions are partial, such as a ban on ground troops, airstrikes and naval operations could continue.

The lower-tensions scenario for Russia and NATO requires a ceasefire in Ukraine, so a guaranteed ceasefire, if reached, meets its first condition. But a guaranteed ceasefire, with Western troops deployed in Ukraine, is a form Russia has openly opposed, so meeting the remaining conditions, new risk-reduction mechanisms and fewer incidents on the eastern flank, could involve more friction than under a ceasefire with only monitors.

The Korean Peninsula issue's external variable of an end to the Russia-Ukraine war and shrinking North Korea-Russia trade first requires an end to the war or a long-term truce, so a guaranteed ceasefire, in which a signed ceasefire holds for a year or more, meets its first condition. The variable's definition does not say how long a long-term truce must last, so treating a ceasefire that holds for a year or more as one is an interpretation. The variable also requires North Korea's exports of troops and shells to stop afterward, so a guaranteed ceasefire alone does not satisfy it.

If a ceasefire with Western troops deployed holds for a year or more, safety concerns, which refugees have cited as the biggest obstacle to going home, ease, so fewer Ukrainians leave for Europe to escape the war and more return. Strong forces also push the other way. If martial-law restrictions on men leaving the country are lifted after a ceasefire, departures to join family abroad or find work could rise for a while, so inflows to Europe could actually grow in the first few years after a ceasefire. The net effect over several years depends on conditions for return, such as jobs and housing, and on when the exit restrictions are lifted.

A guaranteed ceasefire assumes that Britain, France, and other European countries station troops and set up military bases in Ukraine and restock the Ukrainian military's weapons, so the costs of deploying and stationing troops and of replenishing arms raise European defense spending. If the same ceasefire leads to lower tensions between Russia and NATO, a force slowing the growth of defense spending is also at work.

A peace in which Ukraine accepts in writing the legal cession of occupied territory or gives up NATO membership ends the fighting, giving Russia room to rebuild its troops and equipment, and locks in on paper what it won by force. That raises the chance that Russia tests the alliance by seizing part of the territory of NATO's eastern members or launching limited strikes. The Danish and Dutch intelligence assessments cited as evidence concern Russia's capabilities whenever the fighting ends or freezes, so they also apply to a guaranteed or unguaranteed ceasefire; the part specific to peace on Russia's terms rests on the inference that seeing gains rewarded strengthens the intent to attack. The strongest counterargument is that if such a peace includes a halt to NATO enlargement, the threat Russia says it perceives diminishes, which could weaken its motive to test NATO.

If a peace is reached in which Ukraine accepts in writing the legal cession of occupied territory, U.S. allies such as South Korea and Japan will conclude that changing the status quo by force can be rewarded and that U.S. security commitments can become items in deals with great powers, lowering their confidence in U.S. extended deterrence. If the peace involves only a written renunciation of NATO membership, without cession, the effect is smaller. Ukraine is not a U.S. treaty ally, so if allies distinguish between the two cases, this link weakens.

If peace on Russia's terms comes with a phased lifting of sanctions, the discount on Russian crude and its shipping and payment costs shrink, increasing Russia's oil export revenue in dollar terms. The definition of this scenario does not include sanctions relief, so the link is weak if sanctions stay in place, and falling world oil prices as war risk recedes would push the other way. The EU's ban on Russian gas imports is a law, not a sanction, and would not be lifted by peace alone, so gas contributes little to this link.

If lower tensions between Russia and NATO last a year or more, allies gain grounds to slow the planned growth of spending at the defense plan review scheduled for 2029, and the growth of European defense spending slows.
